The absorption of the laser dramatically increases once liquid is formed and increases again once a keyhole vapor column is formed in the liquid. These dramatic fluctuations in power absorption result in instability in laser welding. In contrast, over 90% of electron beam power is absorbed by copper. While the high conductivity of copper makes welding copper challenging, the electron beam process undoubtedly produces the highest quality welds. Significant progress on welding copper using highly absorbing green and blue lasers is being driven by electric mobility applications such as electric vehicles and merits attention in coming years [36]. In 2024, Trumpf consigned a TruDisk 2021 2kW green laser systems to EWI-Ohio for use on research and development projects, specifically focusing on motor and power electronics[37]. Another example of copper EBW includes high power RF windows, which generally include a TiN coating. Since the high temperatures associated with brazing can lead to degradation of the TiN coating, the assemblies are often brazed, TiN coated then EB welded, with an example of CERN’s SPS cavity coupler and the associated EB weld shown below. A hydrogen brazing process uses a back purge of hydrogen as a fluxing agent, reducing oxides and removing hydrocarbon contamination from the surface of the copper. While the vacuum environment of electron beam welding inhibits oxidation, it does not have the beneficial cleaning of the high temperature hydrogen or vacuum environment. The brazing process requires 600°C to 1000°C temperatures sustained for more than 1 hour, which significantly alters the copper microstructure.
